name: Treaty with the Seminole, 1866
promises: Perpetual peace, and in return the United States guaranteed the Seminole quiet possession of their country and protection against hostilities by other tribes (Article 1).

For the cession of the whole Seminole domain, estimated at 2,169,080 acres, the United States would pay $325,362 and the Seminole would receive a new national domain bought from the Creek (Article 3).
A board of commissioners would determine and pay the losses of Seminoles who stayed loyal to the United States during the Civil War (Article 4).
Agency buildings costing up to $10,000 on one section of land that would revert to the nation when no longer used (Article 6).

breaches.what: Article 3 granted the Seminole a 200,000-acre national domain. The Court of Claims found the surveyed tract was 10,351.82 acres short because the western line was run wrongly, that the United States allotted 3,818.21 of those acres to Potawatomi in 1892 and patented the rest to settlers from 1895 to 1913, and held this a taking of Seminole land, valuing it at $7.00 an acre ($72,462.74) plus $130,215.54 as interest.

source.title: Seminole Nation v. United States, Nos. L-51 and L-208, 102 Ct. Cl. 565 (Court of Claims, December 4, 1944)

landTaken: Article 3 ceded the Seminole domain estimated at 2,169,080 acres. The Indian Claims Commission described the domain as 2,037,414.62 acres (Docket 205 findings, 1963).
compensation: The Indian Claims Commission in 1963 found the $325,362 consideration for the 1866 cession was not unconscionable, that all terms of the treaty were carried out, and dismissed the Seminole claim to the $50,000 deducted from that payment for losses of loyal Seminoles and for 1856-treaty annuities withheld in 1862-1866 (Docket 205). In 1962 it had refused to revise the treaty on the ground that the United States forced the Seminole into the Confederacy by withdrawing its troops (Docket 152). In 1944 the Court of Claims found the Seminole entitled to $202,678.28 for the 10,351.82 acres taken from the Article 3 domain (and $221,066.58 in all with an earlier item), but set off a larger sum of gratuitous government spending for the tribe and dismissed the petitions, so nothing was paid (102 Ct. Cl. 565).
today: The Court of Claims held in 1944 that the United States took 10,351.82 acres of the domain this treaty granted, but offsets for government spending cancelled the award and the petitions were dismissed. Separately, the Commission awarded the Seminole Nation a net $34,053.66 in 1958 because the Interior Department, as trustee, failed to cancel the 1920 sale of the 320-acre Emahaka school tract on the national domain when the buyer did not pay (Docket 150). That finding concerns trust management, not the treaty's terms, so it is not counted here as a breach.

nationVoice.summary: In 2022 Senate testimony, Chief Lewis Johnson and Assistant Chief Brian Palmer said Article II of the 1866 Treaty made the Seminole Freedmen citizens of the Nation, that the treaty has never been terminated and still binds both the Nation and the United States, and that the Nation cannot improve its people's condition until the federal government honors its treaties and obligations.

openQuestions: The price per acre the Seminole paid the Creek for the new domain under Article 3 was not checked against the price they received; the Seminole Nation own account of the 1866 terms was not found and should be looked for.
Whether the Curtis Act of 1898 and the Five Tribes Act of 1906 overrode rights in this treaty for the Seminole, who ratified a separate 1897 agreement, was not settled.
Royce lists two cessions under this entry.

The Indian Claims Commission said in 1963 (Docket 205) that all terms of the treaty were carried out; the Court of Claims had already held in 1944 that 10,351.82 acres of the Article 3 domain were taken. The Commission was likely looking only at the consideration and Article 4; the two are recorded as each states.

2026-11-08 sweep: Court of Claims and ICC full text searched for seminole, 1866 and 14 Stat. 755; found Seminole Nation v. United States, 102 Ct. Cl. 565 (1944) (taking of 10,351.82 acres of the Article 3 domain, award cancelled by gratuity offsets) and 316 U.S. 310 (1942). The annuity cases (82 Ct. Cl. 135; 93 Ct. Cl. 500; 316 U.S. 286) concern mainly the 1856 treaty and were not used. Status changed to broken.

plain.promised: Peace and quiet possession of their country, $325,362 for the old Seminole domain, a new 200,000-acre domain bought from the Creek, payment for loyal Seminoles' war losses, and an agency building.
plain.happened: In 1944 the Court of Claims found the United States took 10,351.82 acres of the promised 200,000-acre domain: a wrong survey left them out, and the government gave them to Potawatomi allottees and settlers from 1892 to 1913.
plain.today: The court valued the land and interest at $202,678.28, but set off larger government spending for the tribe, so nothing was paid. The Seminole Nation says the treaty still binds the United States.
